key_insight: At reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces, small polarons move far more slowly than in bulk because surface geometry removes many easy hopping pathways and confines motion mostly to in-plane, inter-row trajectories.
engineering_relevance: This helps explain why porous rutile TiO2 can show much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, which matters for surface-driven devices in catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics from bulk to redox-active oxide surfaces
Simulated oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) over several nanoseconds across temperatures
Compared surface and bulk hopping behavior to quantify mobility suppression
evidence_signal: Nanosecond-scale simulations reveal that surface polaron mobility is suppressed by several orders of magnitude relative to bulk, with rare interlayer hops and vacancy-induced charge localization near oxygen defects.
watch_item: The approach relies on a specific oxide surface model and trained machine-learning dynamics, so transferability to other oxides, defect densities, or reconstructions should be validated before broader use.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
